title: Services & Studio
description: The document-store service layer across SQLite, Postgres and Mongo, with the Studio admin UI

blocks.text: Howl ships an optional service layer: a Mongo-shaped document store with one contract that runs unchanged on SQLite, Postgres, MongoDB, or Redis. @hushkey/service-core owns everything non-storage-specific — validation, an audit/soft-delete envelope, optimistic locking, versioned cache invalidation, timeouts, telemetry. Each backend passes a shared conformance suite, so swapping databases changes a connection, not your code.

rows: The contract: DocumentService, filter grammar, conformance suite.
SQLite via node:sqlite (docs as JSON1). Zero infra — a file on disk.
Postgres (docs as JSONB), with an embedded PGlite fallback for local dev.
Redis as the database (documents + secondary indexes, no modules).

blocks.text: Pick a database in the scaffolder (howl-init) and all of this is wired for you: a connection, a sample items service, and the Studio admin at /studio.
documentSchema() wraps your fields in the full document envelope (id, version, and the audit/soft-delete meta). Define just your domain fields with Zod; the service stamps the rest.
Extend the backend's service class (SqliteService / PgService / MongoService) over one collection — pass the connection, schema, and a collection name. Add domain queries as methods.
The connection itself is created once. SQLite uses node:sqlite; Postgres uses a pg pool (or PGlite when PG_URL is unset); Mongo uses a MongoClient db handle.
Every service exposes the same methods regardless of backend. Writes validate against the schema, bump version, and stamp audit fields; deletes are soft by default.

blocks.text: Queries use a neutral, Mongo-style filter grammar that every backend compiles to its native query — JSONB/JSON1 expressions on the SQL backends, a native filter on Mongo. Dot-paths reach into nested fields.
Supported operators: $eq, $ne, $in, $nin, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $or, $and, $exists — plus dot-path field access.

Next to the filter, find() takes the same shaping options a Mongo client offers: project (which fields come back), sort, collation (locale/case-aware comparison) and hint (which index to use), plus limit/skip. They work on every backend — what differs is how far each one can honor them, which the backend advertises rather than leaving you to guess.

project is Mongo-shaped: 1 includes, 0 excludes, dot-paths reach into sub-documents, and include and exclude cannot be mixed (except id, which rides along with an include projection unless you opt out with { id: 0 }). The older select: ["title"] spelling still works and is deprecated. Projected result sets are cached, but never prefetched into the by-id cache — a partial document must never be served to a later get().

service.findCapabilities reports this per option: native (passed to storage), approximate (honored, but above storage or as a documented subset), or none (accepted and ignored). Under a collation the SQL backends compare values as text — that is what folding case means there — so a collated sort on a numeric field orders lexicographically. SQLite's NOCASE folds ASCII only, and its INDEXED BY is a constraint rather than advice: an unknown or unusable index is an error, and a key-pattern hint is refused.

@hushkey/redis-service treats Redis as the store itself rather than a cache in front of one — the rung of the ladder you climb to for latency. Documents live in Redis as JSON, and the paths you declare in index get a physical secondary index: a SET of ids per value (tag) or a ZSET scored by the value (number). The planner compiles the neutral filter grammar into set operations Redis runs itself.

blocks.text: Every query is correct either way — the index list only decides how much work Redis does. A condition an index cannot answer soundly (a null equality, which must also match absent keys; $ne / $nin / $exists; an undeclared path) narrows nothing and is re-checked against the fetched candidates with the same semantics the SQL backends compile into SQL.

Writes are one round trip: a compare-and-set Lua script that guards on the exact previous document bytes and applies the document and its index changes together — so a document and its indexes can never diverge, optimistic locking is enforced server-side, and a lost race re-reads and re-applies instead of clobbering the other writer. Plain Redis 6.2+ is enough (Valkey, Dragonfly and Upstash too): no RedisJSON, no RediSearch.
Leave the service cache off here (the default). A read is already a memory lookup one hop away — caching in front of Redis buys nothing and adds an invalidation surface.

@hushkey/studio is a Mongo-Compass-style admin UI — one tool across every backend. It speaks the service contract, not the database wire: every write validates, bumps the optimistic-lock version, stamps audit fields, and respects soft delete, like any other caller.

Register any number of services keyed by the name shown in the UI. The dashboard gives you filtered list views, inline card editing, create/edit forms, bulk update and delete, soft-delete and restore, and — on SQL backends — promoted-column introspection with orphan-column cleanup.

The schema view also carries the zero-migration field console: it diffs the live schema against stored documents and lists MISSING fields (declared but absent from old docs) with a one-click backfill of the schema default, and ORPHAN fields (in the JSON but no longer declared) with a one-click drop. So evolving a schema needs no migration script — add a field and backfill it, or remove it and drop it, right from the UI. Works on every backend, document stores included.

The query bar has an OPTIONS row for the same knobs — PROJECT, SORT, COLLATION and INDEX HINT — with field-name completion, a badge counting the active ones, and a per-input note of what the selected backend actually does with it. They travel with paging, refresh and EXPORT, so what downloads matches what you see. A projection that drops id leaves nothing to address a write to, so those rows render read-only.

rows: Map of UI name → service. Null/undefined entries are skipped, so you can register conditionally-connected services without guards.
"standalone" (default) serves a full page; "component" mounts only the JSON API.

daisyUI theme + primary/secondary action classes + extra stylesheet URLs.

blocks.text: In standalone mode the React UI is served from a prebuilt bundle held in memory — no build pipeline needed. In component mode, the middleware mounts only the JSON API and you render <Studio /> from @hushkey/studio/component inside your own dashboard.

Studio is a privileged admin surface. Put it behind your own auth middleware (scoped to /studio) before exposing it in production, and set executionerId from your authenticated user so writes are attributed correctly.
